two-is-greater-than-one.text: Everyone dies the same. I know this for fact, despite never losing anyone. With two pairs of grandparents, two parents, two siblings, and two dogs, it’s easy to imagine everything in life comes in sets of two. Left Twix and right Twix. Green lights and stop signs. Birth and death.
My therapist loves to remind me that there are thousands of ways to die. And sure, that does give me pause, but I need to set this straight.
Everyone dies the same.
Alone? One might inquire. But no, I believe it’s possible to die together.
In pain? That’s not true. Think of the people who die in their sleep.
Is it– The brain suffocates. It runs out of oxygen. And you return to the place from whence you came.

I imagine dying from blood loss as awful and painfully steady. Like riding an escalator that you can clearly see the top of. And while it’s horrid for the person, I can’t help but wonder if the oxygen in their blood rejoices at the sight of the atmosphere, the very air it once called home.
I remember blood. And water. Blood. And water. Boy, and dog; blood, and water. Pouring from my nose to my clothes.
I think I was sitting at the birch-colored IKEA table I never bought. Full of things that became mine.
Black cards. White cards. It’s called “Pillars of Fate”. Spread across the table the way some boys wish they could see me. But I never give them what they want. They get blood. And water.
Water down my throat from a plastic bottle held by spider-web hands. He asks me if I feel light-headed. I stand up.
Clear rushing in, red rushing out. A white paper dam tries to keep the balance, but gets stained in the process. And thrown out.
It’s not water in the brain, it’s metal in the mouth. Tangy, iron-heavy, stifling. But not lethal. Dancing on my tongue because the throat is full, the flow is thick.
He asks me if we should go to the ER. Voice shaky. Eyes round as saucers. I laugh real hard.
He thought I was made out of money. And he’s wrong, but then again, we share an apartment.
And I pay full rent.
Fall in love again and again. Fall in love again and again. Fall in love again and again.
The room is swimming now. My skin may be covered in eczema, but I know it when I see it. It’s full of water.

Cards on the ceiling, dog on the table, my head tilts weird as my vision darkens at the edges, like an old-timey vignette. My eyelids clock out of their shift early, hiding my irises, and leaving my body slack.
For a moment, in the darkness I remember shaking.
Then pushing through the thick velvet, my eyes shed their curtains.
I stare right into his brown-green soul.
And suddenly, dying sounds very scary.
“It’s not a terminal disease.”
“The condition doesn’t decrease life expectancy.”
“It can reduce your quality of life, but there are treatments, medications, and lifestyle changes that you can—”

Believe me, I’ve tried it all. Pills on top of pills on top of pills. It’s easy to mistake my pantry for a pharmacy. But it’s hard to bring myself to use it. One round, white bug, another round, slightly pinkish bug, my personal favorite are the plastic-y little guys that’re the color of wallflowers. Designed for vastly different functions, but once they’re down the hatch, they hurt all the same.

After one such instance, I recall seizing violently, my veins replaced with fire, as I gasped for air on the couch. I wondered if that’s what dying felt like— burning alive. Naturally, I was rushed to the ER and proceeded to writhe in a bed for hours because there were two codes and I wasn’t actively dying. Fair.

As I laid there, shaking uncontrollably, my mind drifted to the other children in the ER. Particularly, why they were there. What had brought them there. How unfair it all seemed. I stared at the smiling fox in the window, as another tremor rocked my body, filling my blood with fire.
Surely, we were all too young to know such pains.
But then again, death doesn’t discriminate.

After many years of online highschool, I felt completely disconnected from the outside world. I had no knowledge of what slang or what clothes was fashionable, no clue as to what was acceptable and what was ‘cringe’. My classmates had traversed time and space, acquiring a coating of lacquer with each hurdle they overcame, each day they conquered. And there I was, soft and dull, at my high school’s graduation day. Four years had passed, and the only thing that had changed was the number in my medical records, labeled ‘AGE:’.

I remember how clearly I could hear my family’s cheers, as I crossed the stage, diploma in hand. Their shouts were so distinct, because there were no others to muddle them. And while my peers snapped group selfies and carpooled to grab Korean BBQ, I walked out of the venue with water in my eyes.

People underestimate the crushing weight of pain. How it mutilates every aspect of your life until you are the smallest you’ve ever been. When this happens, everything stops mattering. And your heart, which has carried you all your life, realizes that no medicine can cure pain. So, it will seek a companion. Because while nothing can make you want to live, a good friend can make it feel worthwhile.

It was freshman fall, when I was young and unfathomably insecure. Slamming myself into a sparkly red dress with not a minute to spare. It was a gala. The Residential College Board Formal. And I was just another girl in the engineering dorm, who’d gotten ready far earlier, but was now running behind.

Initially, I’d selected something elegant and refined; a navy, knee-length dress patterned with golden flowers blooming across the whole of my body. There were ruffles on the sleeves and the collar, and I thought it would be right at home at a gala advertised as a “business casual” affair. Oh, how naive I was.

The moment I stepped into the common room, I thought my cheeks had melted and fallen off my face. Congregating in a few, very colorful clumps, the girls of my dorm reminded me of the Smithsonian’s National Gem Collection— something to be admired, but never touched. At least, not in the hand-me-down dress hanging on my frame.
With a crack, I turned around and bolted out of the common room, scaling two flights of stairs in a storm of fabric and hair. Despite the crisp air, my cheeks still burned like coals.
As I raced down the 4th floor hallway, the homestretch, I passed by a familiar blond boy and screamed, “Kevin, tell them I’ll be down in five!”
I never stopped— just saw a thumbs-up in my periphery. A sign to keep running.

The moment I burst into my room, I threw myself against my closet, wrestling out the only good penny I had to my name. A dress the color of sangria, encrusted in thousands of tiny sequins that danced, even in the dim light of my room. She soaked up the spotlight better than any paid actress.

So, that’s how I got there, practically jumping into my dress, shoving my heels on, and wincing as I pushed a pair of earrings through the skin of my pierced ears. While they’d been closed due to a lack of use, the earrings’ head pins made fast work out of the skin that’d grown back. They stung— I hadn’t worn earrings since the last time I saw my boyfriend, Zach. And that was four months ago.

Eventually, after racing down two flights of stairs— in heels, mind you— I burst into the common room, hiding my frantic breaths. As I clicked and clacked around the room, I noticed a boy sitting on the couch with an oversized backpack— and not an ounce of formalwear. He sat on the couch casually, sporting a grey quarter-zip hoodie and black sneakers.
Prancing up to him, my mouth moved before my brain could react, “So… are you going to the formal?”
“Why wouldn’t I be?” He responded with a smirk, fully aware of his attire.
Embarrassed, I stumbled over my tongue, “Oh— well, I mean… Sorry, it’s just that you don’t seem dressed up like everyone else.”
After all, the other boys in the room were all wearing some form of suit-and-tie— someone was even showing off a three-piece.
“And why would that mean I’m not attending the formal?”
“Uhm…” My whole face turned a shade of red. He was still smiling, so I assumed it was all in good humor. But that didn’t stop my throat from constricting.
Despite my lack of an answer, he laughed, the way wind chimes sound at a beachside villa. Playful and happy. Innocent and clear.
“It’s alright— don’t worry about it! Anyways, I have a surprise in my backpack that’s way more interesting than my hoodie.”
“What is it? Can I guess?”
“Nope! Find me at the formal, and maybe you’ll find out…” He smirked, a glint of mischief in his eyes. I suppressed the urge to roll mine.
And yet, despite my embarrassment, I agreed to meet him again.
Dresses, dancing, party, people. Holding hands. Holding hips. Watch them sway. Silver platters full of food I can’t eat. Ballroom full of people I can’t meet.

Where is that boy, with the brown-green soul? Because everything at this party lives to distance itself. And you’re here, because everyone’s here. And I’m here to drink with my eyes and bleed from my teeth.
I turn a corner and I’m greeted with a tuft of bouncy, curly hair. Dark roast, no creamer.
The owner isn’t clear, just a column of dark fabric against the fuchsia lights. Loading my pistol, I take a shot in the dark.
“Crom?”
There he was, in the flesh. The quarter-zip hoodie and sneakers quickly became history, as he turned towards me. My heart jumped into my throat.
I’d mistaken him for an erudite.
And the longer I stared at his double-breasted suit, shiny dress shoes, and crisp collar, the more I realized how deeply wrong I was.
We went out for sushi. And we don’t eat sushi— but our friends do. So instead of filling our mouths with fish, we told each other stories until we were full.

Laughing while sipping on hot soup, it was easy to forget about our impending exams. We take pictures. You pull out a dozen popsicle sticks, each one a different color, and I pick two: one red, one black. And I say, “It’s me and you.”
The word friend fizzles to the tip of our tongues. It never exits our mouths, because it’s ingrained in our hearts.

It wasn’t long before I was single again— of my own volition. I’d broken things off with my boyfriend, now ex, well before Christmas. And of course, he cried. I said things like I’m sorry and you made such a difference in my life and I was lucky to know you and I know you’ll do great things. And he said, “Is Crom with you right now?”
I said no.
“Did you kiss Crom?”
I said no.
Twice, I only told the truth. But maybe I was missing something. Like giving credit where credit is due. For your brilliant idea: a big thank you.

cinnamon-and-stars.text: Pale, elegant spires pierce the skyline of the most beautiful city in all the world. There is not a single city like Budapest— where the scent of cinnamon waltzes through the cobbled streets, where the sky is akin to the Greek gods and goddesses of old, refusing to bleed anything but lavender and gold. It’s here, in this peculiar city, where my story truly begins.

Though I was thousands of miles away from home, and my mother, they still had a way of worming themselves into the deepest trenches of my mind. The grand city of Budapest was constantly overshadowed by my mother’s beguiling Paris. I have never visited Paris, nor have I ever wanted to. Unruly rodents and even ruder civilians are commodities I do not dream of seeing. To be perfectly frank, there is nothing elegant about gloomy puffs of smoke condescending upon crooked, sickly alleyways. Which is exactly why I love Budapest. Elegance and class seeps out of every nook and cranny within that enchanting dreamscape of a city. And you can certainly trust me, for I’ve seen it all with my own two eyes.
Luckily, this gorgeous city was the first place I’d ever traveled to alone. Indeed, I had never slept in a room that was not my own— it was a bizarre experience to be sure.

Awaking to a posh, pristine place was an oddity in itself. The depressing curtains and equally disinteresting couch of my home were long forgotten memories as I absorbed the essence of the room. Stepping out of bed, I ventured forth through the foreign hotel room, attempting to locate my suitcase in this jungle of color and cotton. The mission at hand was all too easy— its bleak, lifeless form stuck out like a sore thumb. The poor thing looked like a casket at a wedding reception, embarrassingly out of place.

The corpse within the suitcase wasn’t any more exciting; just a gray miasma of wool and all too many wide-legged pants. Suddenly, in this glamorous room, I was hit with a sense of embarrassment. The clothes were perfectly acceptable: professional, simple, and boring. Law abiding— that’s what they were; but then why were they suddenly so undesirable?

A banging at the door threw me out of orbit, “Hello? Mila!” Said a familiar female voice— it was Katiya— her jubilant tone whisking away my insecure thoughts, “It’s time for breakfast! Let’s hurry!” A few other voices I couldn’t perfectly recognize chimed in, probably spurred by their grumbling stomachs. “Alright, alright! I’ll be out soon!” I exclaimed as I sprinted toward the bathroom, trying to get ready as quickly as possible.

Now one might be wondering why these young hooligans were hollering at my door at the crack of dawn, and I must say I too was mildly surprised. Even though this bunch of Russian youths were simply people I was assigned to stick with, we all got along fabulously. The lot of us were young professionals around my age, each of them here in Budapest to represent the company they worked for. This unique trip was also a way for young professionals to network and experience other areas of the expansive USSR; most importantly though, it was free (thanks to the government)!

After my groupmates’ abrupt wake-up call, I flew through my morning routine. In a snap, I was strolling along Budapest’s scenic streets migrating towards our selected breakfast spot. It was a warm, homey cafe not far from our hotel, its wood accents reminding me of the grand mountains that resided over my quaint home town. Even its color pallet looked as if it had been transported straight from home, with an array of majestic, earthy tones.

The cafe’s mysterious fragrance, though, was as foreign as it was fitting— its scent as tender as a mother’s embrace and yet as intricate as the hand-sewn rhinestones of a privileged woman’s dress. Not only that, but it also had deep, earthy qualities married to a bright undertone as thin and sharp as a needle— which pricked one’s nostrils upon contact. The unknown fragrance overwhelmed my senses, so thoroughly that it left me utterly and completely breathless.

Keeping this torrent of emotions to myself, I calmly walked into the magical cafe before me. Filing in behind my other groupmates, I gawked at the menu— elegantly scripted on the massive chalkboard behind the barista. It was as if the wonderful fragrance had seeped itself into the cafe and even its barista, giving both a soft, comforting aura. Approaching the counter at last, I sheepishly asked the doll-eyed barista about the decadent aroma of the cozy cafe. “Oh, the smell?” She chirped, her Hungarian accent brushing against her words, “It’s just the cinnamon from the buns. Yummy, isn’t it?” I nodded, already whisked away by a train of thought…

Cinnamon. Its name was as romantic as its aroma. With no hesitation, I ordered their glorious cinnamon buns, plus the thing called ‘Espresso’ on their menu— because why not? If these delicacies could be as attractive as this phenomenal spice, I just knew I had to try them all.

“Mila!” The sweet barista exclaimed, a tray with my order in-hand. Thanking her, I sat down in a rush, already salivating over the treats that lay before me. I smiled down at the two treats, my giddy anticipation sending shocking slivers of lighting straight to my fingertips. I was simply over the moon with ecstasy! Gently, as if it was porcelain, I brought the puffy cinnamon roll to my lips. Its holy fragrance filled my nose, as I sunk my teeth into the tender morsel, drinking in its magical essence. Its ichor tasted like nothing else I’d ever feasted upon, while earthy undertones caressed my tastebuds. The sickly sweet frosting overwhelmed my senses, as I enjoyed this foreign, forbidden fruit— devouring every bit of its pale, pillow-soft flesh. It felt so wrong that I was confident I’d be banished from Eden. Or was this homeland, this Republic of so-called equality, a beguiling prison?

After our delightful breakfast, we headed towards the building of the government-run organization who was sponsoring this trip to meet up with our assigned tour guides. Together we were a fresh, lively group numbering a dozen total— eight eager, wide-eyed Russians and four jovial Hungarians as our guides. Seen as all of us were young adults, we traveled quickly, with a bounce in our step as we set off for a bout of sightseeing.

It’s a funny thing, sightseeing. We meander around things so much bigger and grander than us, awe-ing and ooh-ing at the picturesque sights. I simply don’t understand it. Yes, the structures are pretty and all, but what about the culture, the environment? A truly beautiful city is one that is beautiful on the outside and inside— a beauty that’s reflected in its people and general buildings. My mother always said Paris was the most romantic of places; we disagreed on a lot of things. Of course, the Eiffel Tower will forever be alluring— but the city itself? Quite the opposite. Paris should honestly become synonymous with ‘smoky tourist trap’ instead of ‘love’. The alleys are dirty and shallow, just like the people, for how does one expect a city to gain the title ‘The Capital of Pickpocketing’ while having lovely citizens? I refuse to fall for that beguiling mirage of a destination. Meanwhile in Budapest, the shops and such aren’t absorbed by touristy fakes but genuinely sell the most gorgeous of wares. Gone are the drab, mass-produced garbs from Russia— my heart now sung for those garments of whimsy found only in boutiques. Thus, while everyone was marveling at the grandeur of the Statue of Saint Stephen within Halaszbastya church, I was itching to return back to those cobbled streets from before. The stone of the monuments was dead silent, while the vivacious spirit of the city whispered in my ear like the Serpent himself. On the fringes of this red Eden-republic, the tree of good and evil was all mine for the taking.

We strolled around the statue, quietly chattering amongst ourselves as we soaked in the peace and calm of the church. Falling into step next to the main guide, I innocently asked about the schedule, as the day was still quite young and naive. Turning towards me he quickly recapped the day’s schedule: sightseeing, free time, lunch, more sightseeing (this time the Parliament building), and then dinner. I’m sure there were more intricacies to it, but the object of my current obsession was undoubtedly those boutiques we’d passed by. Their glass storefronts reminded me of an expensive jewelry box, the kind with a dancing ballerina figure in center. It was a novelty I had scarcely laid eyes on, for the only glass boxes I’d seen were the ones in grocery stores back home. They were used to cover and ‘protect’ the produce from hungry customers, as if all of us were filthy criminals that couldn’t even be trusted with a sack of potatoes. The people were a thing to be feared.

When freetime rolled around, I decided to break off from the group and explore the city on my own. It was a bit reckless of me, but I didn’t mind a bit— for that was the price of complete freedom. Wandering through this forest of cobble and brick, I followed the Danube River with a single goal in mind: to find the perfect boutique. But did such a thing even exist?

After searching around for an hour, I had found the crown jewel of my wildest fantasies. Its exterior was just as gorgeous as the others, but its heart was what drew me in. While many of the other boutiques were realms of grace and whimsy, almost disengaged from the world, this particular spot was sleek and ultra-modern. The boutique’s glassy eyes were tinted over, adding a glint of mystery to their murky depths. Like a moth with a streetlight in its sights, my feet moved on their own, gliding straight through its front door with no hesitation. Inside, my attention frantically fluttered around the shop, the reality of my limited time crashing down on me. I needed something beautiful but restrained, something unique but also legal; this woman surely didn't want to get thrown out of Eden. Pausing, a thought slithered into my head: perhaps, I was just another cog in the machine, molded by the government. It made sense, after all we honestly looked identical in our bleak, conservative garments. Unsurprisingly, they reduced crowds of individuals into one homogenous, gray blob; the general public, looking as if it had been manufactured in an assembly line. The great government was probably hoping the machine would run smoother with uniformity on its side. We were forced to dress a certain way, act a certain way— for what? Why does a government get to decide that for its people? What kind of twisted Eden was this republic?

The psychological dam that held back all of my questions and doubts shattered into smithereens— thoughts flooded my mind, drowning everything else out. I suddenly despised my suitcase and everything inside of it; my own clothes felt as if they were burning into my skin like a brand, painful reminders of the confusing place I called home. It hurt, but I knew I couldn’t leave— this republic was my home after all, and I couldn’t imagine leaving my family and friends. And rebelling? My heart skipped a beat at the thought of such a dangerous act. I knew all too well that opposition was futile, the only things gained would not be freedom or liberty— but simply a shattered dream and a broken body. We the people were weak, defenseless sheep with no way to control the very monster we had welcomed in. Truthfully, no matter how upsetting the government was I wouldn’t dare to stand in its way. That would surely be suicide.

A deep sigh escaped my lips, the depressing thoughts weighing heavily on my mind as I sullenly browsed through the once-magical boutique. It was as if my joy had been mercilessly vacuumed up, transforming the store into a dry husk of its former self. I unenthusiastically scanned through the store and turned to leave, my drab shoes screeching to a halt when I saw the piece of art displayed next to their counter.

A bottomless umbra, that’s what it was, consuming every ray of light that dared to even get close. The boutique melted away as I got lost in this dress’s obsidian depths. It was akin to staring up at a clear, moonless sky— its inky depths enveloping my eyes in a peaceful, timeless embrace. A smattering of stars blessed this obscure night sky with elegance and otherworldly class. Their rhinestone bodies heavily populated the bottom portion of the dress, becoming scarce past the waist. The dress itself was simple but powerful— like using one classy word to describe a plethora of complex emotions. Its elusive fabric clung to the wearer’s top half, exposing their curves in a minorly risque but elegant way— with an extended collar and long sleeves to match. I had to try it on.

Now clear as day, my mind organized itself. Rule follower— that’s what I was. My intention wasn’t to suddenly rebel like an imbecile, I simply desired to carve out my own individual existence, however risqué or odd that was. Gazing upon myself, clad in this midnight masterpiece, I realized there was a way to find harmony between both my individual wishes and the government’s oppressive will. It was the perfect balance: monochromatic, no cut-outs, and dark coloring; but also tight, posh, and just slightly bejeweled. This dress wasn’t a compromise with the government—  this was my personality— it took advantage of the gray space provided. New dress in hand, I flew out of the boutique, back into the shining streets of Budapest, glimmering with the confidence of a thousand stars. This was my story to tell, my future to build— and most certainty— my dress to wear.

hamartia.text: The Shadows
The man with the deep, cerulean eyes left without a word. In his wake, the front door slammed close, rattling on its hinges. The exchange had been heated, to say the least.
A young man sighed heavily as he walked away from the front door, his many hanging earrings clinking in the thick silence that followed the abrupt departure.

That ocean-eyed man had a name— Arlo— but honestly, the young man wished he could scrub it from his memory after their recent altercation. Arlo was a slick, wickedly-sharp instrument with an awful penchant for perfection. Rarely did the young man ever see the beating heart that lay beneath those meticulously dry-cleaned suits. Once a close friend, he now walked a path so far removed from the young man’s that he personally struggled to even grasp his trajectory. Truly, Arlo Soven was an enigma.

And if Arlo was an ingenious cipher cracker-and-creator, then the young man— X— would be a colorful, fruity cocktail. Seemingly harmless, but every bit as eye-catching. He was a foolhardy, fun-loving being that lit up every room he was in— the life of every photoshoot and party he attended. X never missed a beat. Much like the drink in question, he strived to be as palatable as possible— in every sense of the word, from his personality to his appearance. X was so good at this that everyone who met him could only gossip about how he was such sinfully sweet eye candy. And in X’s eyes, that was true power.

But like many alcoholic drinks, X had an afterburn— a sunless side that only Arlo quietly noticed. Though no matter how close Arlo got, that side would never spare him a single glance. Not even when they fought, which they did all too often over everything from where to get takeout from (always Marabella versus Paper Rabbit) to what should be done about the Spark Separation Act (SSA). An incredibly controversial law, tensions in South Korea were at an all time high as the SSA was approaching its 100th anniversary.

X hated how Arlo’s last speech at an anti-SSA rally still rang in his ears: “The SSA is an excuse made by the Bright and the powerful to take advantage of the Dim and the weak. Being unable to run as fast as the wind or shoot electricity from our fingertips shouldn’t disqualify us from employment opportunities and higher education. Our country needs to wake up and realize that might doesn’t make right.”

Dozens of thoughts flooded his mind as X collapsed onto his plush couch and ran his hands through his long hair. For a while, he rested there, his damp eyes trained on the blank ceiling, with one hand clutching his cell phone and the other still mindlessly playing with his hair. It cascaded off his shoulders like dozens of silky, inky tributaries that only seemed to multiply endlessly— there was no end, no right choice.
‘To fight or not to fight, to call or not to call… damnit Arlo.’

runs.text: ‘To fight or not to fight, to call or not to call… damnit Arlo.’

hamartia.text: Then, as hesitant as a rabbit, he slowly opened his list of contacts and dialed. As the phone worked, X winced at the bold white letters that glared back at him: ‘Arlo Soven’.
The nervous rapping of his fingers against the coffee table could be heard throughout the house, filling the tense air just enough until a voice popped up. X held his breath.

“Hello. You’ve reached Arlo Soven. Sorry for the inconvenience, but I’m not available right now. Please leave a message with your name and intent— I will get back to you as soon as possible. Thank you.”
BEEP.
Immediately, X’s head started spinning as he haphazardly tried to craft a response, but in the end, his thumb silently slammed into the red button at the bottom. He exhaled a defeated sigh.

“What the h*ll is there to say?” X muttered under his breath, “I have a job to keep and an appearance to maintain. How can you expect me to drop everything for your radical dreams?” Clearly, his blood was still boiling from the abrupt departure.

X knew there was no one around to hear his words, but they served as more of a reminder than anything else. Because in the back of his mind, another part of him was already busy looking through his schedule for a time to visit Arlo’s apartment. Somehow, there was a slot tomorrow after a modeling photoshoot with one of South Korea’s hottest luxury brands: Veloure. Just the name made his skin prickle with anticipation.

As X begrudgingly slipped into his bed, he pulled out his phone. Its bright, fluorescent light painted his face eerily pale, as he quickly opened his messages and began typing: ‘is it alr if i stop by tmr? like 11am? or is another time better? should i pick up lunch from Marabella?’
‘No, what in the world am I saying?’

runs.text: ‘No, what in the world am I saying?’

hamartia.text: X blankly stared at the screen for a while, mulling over his pathetically passive language.
‘I have every right to be mad.’

runs.text: ‘I have every right to be mad.’

hamartia.text: Deleting his former message, he instead typed up: ‘hey, let’s meet tmr, i wanna talk. 11am at ur place.’
Again, he stared at the screen. And again, he deleted it.
Not a single word felt right.

After many minutes of silence, his phone shut off with a disappointing click, and the room plunged into darkness; not even the city lights dared to pierce through the curtains. The darkness enveloped X like a thick, warm blanket, soaking up his tears and lulling him into a deep, dreamless slumber.
The Prey

Sunlight sliced through the car windows, so intense that it warmed X’s face and mercilessly burned his eyes. No matter. He quickly flicked on his sunglasses and continued staring out at the glass jungle that everyone called Seoul. All the buildings were clad in their own kind of haute couture that glowed under the sun’s rays. Who needs a fantastic silhouette when you can simply light up the whole room?
X wistfully sighed under his breath— he wished modeling was that straightforward.

As the car began to slow, at a red light, his view suddenly became congested by a crowd of multi-colored blobs, each of them holding up a phone in front of them. Some waved, others shook envelopes or gift bags excitedly, and even more started exclaiming something. Quickly, he looked through the other window, expecting to see a celebrity or something of the sort crossing the street.
But there was nothing but asphalt and moving cars.
This was his stop, the site of the photoshoot. And the people, well, they were calling out his name.

X quietly cursed under his breath, his head spinning at the thought of interacting with so many people. Or should he say: fans. Like the flick of a switch, his heart started rattling against his rib cage. He’d have to track down the leaker another time.
‘In a few minutes, it’ll all be over,’ he tried to reassure himself, while taking a few deep breaths.

runs.text: ‘In a few minutes, it’ll all be over,’
he tried to reassure himself, while taking a few deep breaths.

hamartia.text: Just as he reached for the door handle, his manager’s concerned voice rang out from the passenger’s seat, “Hey, we can go around and pull up to the back of the building, X. You really don’t have to go out there.”
X flashed Eunmi, his manager, a smile despite his shaky, sweaty hands. “Nope, I’ll meet you at the lobby in a bit. Just tell ‘em I’ll be like, five minutes late!”
“Wait a second, I’ll call security—”

Too late. X was already basking under the sun, glowing brighter than all the other skyscrapers around. He couldn’t help but smile at the enthusiastic crowd— their energy was simply infectious. X sprinted towards them, ignoring the anxious butterflies in his stomach, and began collecting the letters, gift bags, and plushies they all had. Internally, he really didn’t understand the cause for celebration, but he thanked them all the same, so many times that the words became foreign syllables to his ears.

The crowd pressed against him like a wave— crashing inwards, then slowly pulling away, again and again. However, it was so much louder than any beach he’d ever been to. And everyone had their phones out.
“Oh my gosh, X! I love you!” One would exclaim, then another would interject, “Wait, I have something for you!” And of course, there was the forceful, “Get outta my way! Lemme see him—”

But by far, the worst question of all came from the people with mics and cameras bigger than his head, “Hey X, we’re big fans! Can you tell us your thoughts on the radical politician, Arlo Soven? Is it true that you two are dating?”
He tried his best to ignore those people.
It all became a dizzying jumble of requests and questions, and more requests and more questions until he felt like his brain was going to combust.
‘But they love you, why stop them? Besides, one wrong move and you’re finished,’ his conscious whispered, coaxing him into submission.

hamartia.text: It worked, for a little, until a fan stuffed a big bouquet of flowers into his arms— they were gorgeous, laden full with sun-gold petals. The flowers were so large that X had to use two arms to cradle the bouquet. As he stopped to admire them, he quickly recognized what they were: sunflowers in full bloom.

And it all came crashing down. X had something to settle with someone, and that certain someone happened to love these flowers and these flowers only. On top of that, there was still the photoshoot to complete. Dread filled his stomach— he was going to be late.

“I’m really sorry everyone, but I gotta go! I have a shoot to get to—” X exclaimed as loudly as he could, but the human wave kept crashing down on him. Even as he tried to gently push back, a legion of phones completely shielded his view of the photoshoot building— there was no path forward.

“Please,” X mumbled, pulling his cap down over his eyes. All the cameras and phones were making him nauseous. He really couldn’t wait to see this all over his Seera feed in an hour. But a thought made him pause.
‘Why are there so many fans here?’

hamartia.text: He came to this building multiple times a week, but to see this many fans was rare.
“Excuse me! What’s your opinion on the SSA?”
“Hello, X? Are you deaf? I said—”

Suddenly, under the sun’s bright eye, X felt unbelievably cold. Dark, twisted hands grasped his heart from the inside, like a deadly viper delivering the killing blow. It was his power, his Spark. It had smelled weakness and struck without hesitation knowing that he lacked the willpower to control it. A cold sheer spread over his pupils and X surely didn’t need a mirror to know their new color: vermillion. Thank goodness it was covered by the cap… for now.
This little fact didn’t offer him much solace. He could hear his frantic heart pounding in his ears, desperately flailing like a dying animal, but X knew it was pointless.
Its beating was slowing.
They were all going to see him now— at his worst, at his ugliest.
‘Take me away.’
Nothing. X just stood there, swallowing the crowd’s confused and bitter stares whole. They burned him inside and out, like he was standing in a pit of flames getting hot coals shoved down his throat.

Deep down, X felt like he deserved all of this. Not only was he unable to deal with a crowd, as a rising star no less, he also had carelessly let his closest friend slip through his fingers just yesterday. A spectacular failure, no doubt, for he knew Arlo like the back of his hand, and yet, all that knowledge amounted to nothing when faced with that dreadful question:
“Will you stand with me?”
Silence ensued, tears were shed. X didn’t even try to stop Arlo as he stormed away, slamming the front door behind him.

As shame and regret washed over X dark, translucent tendrils suddenly rose up around him. In the blink of an eye, they twisted around him and widened, shielding him from all the prying eyes. The tendrils tightened their form, pressing closer and closer. Even though it felt foreign, X embraced it.
The darkness, the cold— it made him blissfully numb as his throat began to close, his vision started to swim, and his heartbeat slowed to a halt.
‘Take me home.’
As if on command, light flooded his vision, burning away the darkness.
The Kill
A familiar, but unusually unlocked door. A dining room straight out of a magazine. A man with cerulean eyes, already expecting him.

That’s all X remembered after suddenly teleporting to Arlo’s apartment. Now, he was sitting in awkward silence at Arlo’s dining table, watching as Arlo displayed an array of fresh, pulsating tears on his back.
“My Spark— it’s consuming me,” Arlo stated, frank as ever; like it was a bland fact and nothing more. There was no ‘Hello’ or ‘I hate you,’ just the plain truth.
X scoured Arlo’s bare back, his eyes widening at the sight of all the carnage.

If the nape of his neck was a mountain, then the scars were rivers of golden snowmelt, flowing down the length of his spine and branching out like a delta. His shallow breaths were the only reminder to X that those glowing rifts were born of flesh and power— not a pen. Had Arlo stopped breathing, his back could’ve been mistaken for a map.
‘Never,’ X thought, for he hoped that Arlo’s chest would never cease to rise and fall, no matter how many governments he opposed or crimes he committed.

His eyes began to burn and sting at the edges, as he continued to stubbornly stare down the death message before him. Or maybe he was just trying to distract himself from the rising guilt in his chest. After all, he’d completely shut Arlo down the other day.
After what felt like eons, Arlo scoffed, “I know that silence.”
He looked straight into X’s obsidian irises and hissed, “Does it feel good? To know that your hands and ‘appearance’ will stay clean because I’m finishing the job myself?”

His words were laced with venom and his vicious eyes sliced into X’s own. The tension in the room quickly became palpable as they both stood there, eye to eye, with a thousand unspoken words between them. X opened his mouth, then quickly thought better of it. His fingers twitched under Arlo’s glare— he wouldn’t be surprised if he melted right then and there. Casting his gaze to the floor, X hid his watering eyes.
“Hah,” Arlo seethed. “Not going to even spare a word for your dying friend? Or am I now just an enemy to you—”
“Stop,” X whispered, like a soft breeze, a fragile thing.
“What? Can’t handle the truth?”
X thought he heard something shatter as he screamed, “Shut the h*ll up!”
His voice cracked like porcelain under the effort of keeping his tears back. The brief silence that followed left a ringing noise in both their ears.
Snapping back into character, Arlo smirked as X started again.
“You.” Hands shaking, X pointed his index finger at Arlo. “You know the damn truth! After all, who’s been your closest friend for over a decade?”
“And yet you never followed… or even apologized.”
Before Arlo could even flinch, foreign hands were at his shoulders, shoving him into the back of the chair.

“Damnit Arlo!” X gasped, blood pounding in his ears, “I did it for you. I did it all for you! I only said no to stop you because I knew you’d take whatever you’re planning too far. But I should’ve known that you stop for no one, not even your—”

“Don’t feed me that crap! The only person you did it for was yourself! You were afraid people would find out that you’re conspiring with a radical who disagrees with the very foundation of this filthy country. Stop pretending to be a victim, X. The only thing you are is a spineless, heartless person.”

Arlo hissed, leaning into X— their faces a mere inch apart. His cerulean eyes looked like a raging blue fire, razing everything in its path, fueled by a terrible rage— and the bloody pieces of a broken heart.
‘Say that you care about him,’ X’s inner conscience urged, ‘say that you only wanted him to live.’

hamartia.text: X shook his head, pushing those thoughts as far away as possible. His skin crawled. There were a thousand excuses he could make, but only one answer to give.

“I—” abruptly cutting off, X stopped to take a breath. His throat constricted on itself like a boa, trying desperately to keep the words from leaving his mouth. Even the butterflies in his stomach were laughing at him— he looked like a dead fish, with his mouth agape as he struggled to say another word. How easy it would be to lie…
‘But Arlo deserves the truth.’

“You’re right, Arlo. I only know how to run, how to preserve myself and my face. And honestly, that’s all I’ve ever done. I ran from the orphanage, from law enforcement— and now from you. I am so sorry… for not being there when you needed me the most.”

Arlo’s scowl wavered, his narrowed eyes widening in shock for a moment. But it wasn’t long before he covered it all up with a distrustful glare, as if X’s words were too good to be true, too pure for this twisted world.
X released his grip and stepped back silently, giving Arlo space. His cold features now betrayed little emotion, other than his Adam’s apple, which bobbed like a fishing buoy.

That was X’s cue to walk away and brew a peace offering: valerian root tea. He turned and gave Arlo one last remorseful look before heading off to the kitchen, never mind that this was Arlo’s place and not his own.

X found the teapot with ease, after all, he’d been here just a few days ago, eating take-out and laughing at Arlo’s horrible dad jokes. With a heavy sigh, he filled the teapot, set it on the stove, and went to the pantry to find some tea sachets. But abruptly, he froze. There was already a sachet and two teacups next to the stove, along with a familiar, honey-colored journal: Arlo’s diary. It reeked of imaginary laws, childhood memories, and long-forgotten liveliness. Of life.
‘Arlo is dying,’ he paused, staring blankly at the kitchen’s stark white backsplash. X dared not question how, for it was evident enough from the scars that it was related to his Spark.

Much like earlier when he’d faced that mob of fans, his control over his Spark was slipping quickly as his mind spiraled down, down, down. Suddenly, breathing became difficult.
CLICK.

The stove in front of him burst to life, its tiny flames licking the sides of the teapot with fervor. X staggered backwards, the adrenaline from his panic episode quickly melting away into fatigue. He tried leaning on the countertop, but the moment he took a deep breath, exhaustion filled his limbs from head to toe.

hamartia.text: The Decay

A loud crash came from the kitchen and, instinctually, Arlo jumped up from his chair. Adrenaline shot through his veins, numbing his concoction of emotions as he sprinted to the kitchen. A sliver of fear sent shivers down his spine, but he brushed it off, knowing all too well how quickly it could overtake him.
The teapot had reached a boil, its screeches echoing through the apartment like cruel jeers, spurring Arlo forward. There was no ounce of hesitation in his steps as he dashed into the kitchen.

By the time he got there, the teapot’s screaming had reached a feverish pitch. As Arlo looked down, he witnessed a scene that could’ve come straight out of an intrusive thought: X, plastered on the floor, shaking with the effort of trying to sit upright.

“Whoa, slow down there,” X chuckled lightly, despite the rivulets of blood dribbling down his face. He continued, unable to look up at Arlo, “Look, I’m fine— can you just move that kettle off the heat?”

But Arlo was already there, flicking the stove off and staring down at X, his expression unreadable. The longer X watched, the more those ice-blue eyes slowly melted into an endless ocean, bluer than the blue sky above.
‘Damn,’ marveled X, ‘I really missed those eyes.’

Maybe the blood loss was getting to him, but he swore Arlo’s ocean eyes could send him straight to the Bahamas with just a glance. Stare at them too long, and X knew he’d find himself drowning under warm, sapphire waves.
X was so distracted that he didn’t notice Arlo’s finger under his chin, swiveling his head from side to side. Arlo was busy inspecting the nasty gash on X’s forehead, dutifully examining the damages.

“I know you must be wondering how I’m… dying,” Arlo started, hesitant to break the silence, “and it’s complicated. But I know you want an answer, so I’ll put it like this: something… horrible… I did in my youth has finally caught up to me.”
Arlo wrung his hands ever so slightly— he’d seldom seen X this silent before.
But he steeling his nerves, he stated, “I Empowered my Spark.”
The kitchen grew so quiet, they could hear each other’s quivering breaths.
“What?” X finally whispered in disbelief, “I’ve only heard of that in fairytales? How?”
But Arlo just shook his head, keeping that secret to himself.

“When I was younger I constantly felt… powerless. There was just so much injustice happening around me and there was nothing I could do about it. After all, my Spark could only create barriers— but physical protection can’t protect your rights. That’s when I decided to become a lawyer. But, if you remember, I got rejected from every law school simply because my Spark was too Dim.”
“Right… It was horrible.” X nodded, as memories from that fateful day resurfaced— it was the first time he’d ever seen Arlo cry.

“But I was determined to prove them wrong, to prove that I was capable of becoming a lawyer. So I Empowered my Spark and destroyed my body… for people I hated with every fiber of my being. And yet, they rejected me again.”
Arlo fell silent and resumed his work, his pale lips pressed into a hard line. Just as Arlo attached the last bandage in place, X— his eyes watering— blurted out, “I should be dying in your place.”

Suddenly, X felt a pair of warm arms wrap around him, as the all-too-familiar bergamot filled his nose. He rested his head onto Arlo’s shoulder and tightly clutched onto his torso, hugging him back— so afraid that Arlo would disappear again and leave a trail of blue flames behind him. X melted into Arlo’s embrace; the gentle calm only broken by choking sobs and frequent sniffles.

Arlo could almost hear the sound of X’s heart shattering into a thousand bloody pieces. They lodged themselves deep within Arlo’s own chest, slicing at his willpower. X could just barely see the doubt cross Arlo’s face, his hard lips and furrowed brows telling all. For the first time in a long time, Arlo could hear questions poking through his carefully crafted path.
“I— I have to go,” he announced, rather briskly, breaking the hug and practically leaping from the floor. He had to get away as soon as possible— for X’s undoing was undoing him too.
Hurt by his abrupt push, X slowly, as if each word was its own sentence, whispered, “You’re not telling me something, Arlo Soven.”
X was met with deafening silence; Arlo didn’t even dare to look into his ebony eyes. Instead, he continued to stare at the front door, while absent-mindedly fidgeting with his watch
But in the silence, X caught wind of Arlo’s lost words.
‘You, Arlo Soven— the perfect logic machine, the boy I’ve known for a dozen years— are scared of me?’

hamartia.text: Betrayal sent a sharp pang through his heart— it stung. He felt like reality had just slapped him in the face… or maybe it was just Arlo. Looking up from the frigid kitchen floor, X could almost see a barrier rebuilding before him, golden and translucent. A twin to the real ones Arlo could make with his Spark— and just as unbreakable.
‘Hah, guess we can never be kids again.’

hamartia.text: The False Calm Before

Back then, they were thick as thieves. When Arlo wasn’t studying, he was bounding over rooftops with X, searching for the perfect spot to admire the Seoul sunset. And whenever X tried to study (he was a chronic truant), Arlo was there too— pointing out mistakes and flicking his forehead whenever he’d lose focus.

Arlo was even there when X filed to officially change his name. Abandoned on a bitter autumn day, X arrived at the orphanage with no name— so the head of the orphanage, logically, just marked an X over the spaces that were supposed to be his first and last name. It stuck— until a fifteen-year-old Arlo found out and exclaimed, “How is anyone ever going to hire you?!”
“What do you mean? What’s wrong with it?”

“First, I’ll talk about what a name really is. Your name is your second face, an identifier but also a necessary accessory. A good name compliments you before you open your mouth, convinces employers that you have a respectable lineage, and—”
“But I like being X!”

‘It’s a singular letter at best, a chicken scratch at worst. He clearly loves it though. But no one will take him seriously.’ Arlo pondered, thinking hard on how he could convince X to change his name.

hamartia.text: He paced a bit, his leather loafers clacking against the school’s rooftop. X watched on with curiosity while munching on the banh mi sandwich Arlo had brought for him. To be frank, Arlo always brought him lunch, so this was nothing new.

Stopping abruptly, Arlo pivoted towards X. Eyes alight with a whisper of a smile, Arlo started, “I have an idea: we can change your official name on paper, but you can keep asking everyone to call you X. That way, when you put in job applications, they won’t reject you just because of your name.”
X sputtered, trying not to laugh at Arlo’s enthusiasm over something as trivial as a name. Oftentimes, he felt like Arlo cared more about his future than he did.
“Okay Mr. Businessman!” X smirked, so sure that Arlo would be stunned by his next remark, “If you have all the answers, what should my name be?”
But not a moment passed before Arlo announced proudly, “Yujin. Ahn Yujin, to be precise.”
It was as if he’d been preparing for this moment ever since he’d first laid eyes on X.
Because Arlo absolutely had.
The Storm
Awkwardly, Arlo stumbled towards the dining room table. His unreadable eyes didn’t quite match his hard lips and clenched fists.

The air was taunt as a bowstring. Gaze locked on the front door, he walked briskly, like he was late to some imaginary meeting. Leaving, Arlo was leaving. Far away. Almost at the door knob. Just a breath until—

“Stop!” X commanded, as the same dark, translucent tendrils from the fan ‘meeting’ materialized out of every shadow in the room. They instantly wrapped around his limbs, holding him in place. X could feel Arlo fighting against his grip— albeit in vain. Because if Arlo’s Empowered Spark was a sea, X’s Spark was the whole sky. And X hated that with every fiber of his being. Yet, as a cold sheer once again spread over his pupils, not a shred of guilt was left in him.
“Look at me, Arlo Soven.”
His head didn’t move an inch.
“You’re not leaving me again—” X’s voice cracked, a sob escaping his lips, “until you explain yourself. Why are you pushing me away? Just let me help you—”
“Never.” It wasn’t oceans that met X’s gaze, but cerulean slits.
X gritted his teeth, sorrow freezing over into frustration.
“Let me make this right.”
Silence.
But that wasn’t an answer he was willing to swallow. Again. So, he stormed up to Arlo, so close he could almost taste the smell of sea salt, bergamot, and X’s own blood on his shirt.

The air crackled between them, two wills colliding. A silent war. The ocean pushed against the night. With every tide, it sharpened itself like a weapon. Except the bottomless night stayed resolute, consuming every offensive with ease.
Sweat beaded on Arlo’s brow. The ocean was slipping into the night, its grip loosening and loosening, until only the void, the starless night, was left.

“I always wanted your help, always wanted you on board. Even after you refused my offer, I was already making elaborate plans to get you involved, one way or another,” Arlo stated, sharp and rushed, “that’s why I sent the mob of fans, why I left my door purposefully unlocked… But the moment I saw you, I knew.”
“Knew wh—”
“I knew I couldn’t use you! That’s the real reason why I acted so hostile, bitter, and angry towards you earlier. I just… couldn’t bear to make you a pawn in my sick, dangerous game.”
Pupils wide with shock, X’s skin began to crawl. In the silence that followed, Arlo’s eyes had turned sullen and remorseful, dulling in color.
“I had it all planned out— your role, your persona, your every move— even the other pieces you’d kill.”
Arlo squeezed his eyes shut for a moment, each word was a struggle to utter. Fear had his heart in a chokehold.
“It’s disgusting, I know. You’re free to hate me from now on, free to burn every picture of us, free to tell me to get out of your life.”

Arlo smiled sadly, “I’m not going to be a part of it for much longer anyways. While I’m still going through with my plan, it’s going to be without you. Please accept that as my apology. I can’t give you much more than that… I’m sorry.”

X softened ever so slightly at Arlo’s apology— goodness knows they were as rare as diamonds. He mulled it over in his head as he watched Arlo have a staring contest with the floor. It was intense— his knotted eyebrows, gritted teeth, and fiery gaze said it all. Rage consumed the air around Arlo, crackling like a fire pit.
And X walked right into it.

Instantly, the dark tendrils receded, freeing Arlo. X gently rested a shaky hand on Arlo’s chest. Each heartbeat was the note of a song he could sing in his sleep, a hymn that he hummed on hard days, a tune that took him home.
‘I know this heart,’ X said to himself, ‘I’ve known it for a long time,

hamartia.text: Determination shimmered in X’s eyes, as he locked gazes with Arlo, “Hear me out, but the world needs you.”
Sputtering, Arlo interjected, “What? But you don’t even know—”
“I don’t need to know exactly what you’re going to do, because I know that whatever it is, it’s doing good in the world.”
Arlo raised an eyebrow, confused by his friend’s sudden confidence.
“This makes no logical sense. How can you make such a conclusion without tangible evidence?”

X smirked knowingly, as he remarked, “That’s not true, there’s definitely evidence. You only protect people with your Spark’s barriers. You have always despised this country and the way it discriminates against people with dimmer Sparks. And on top of that…”
As his voice trailing off, X took a deep breath before uttering, “You loved me, even though I didn’t know love and had none to give in return.”
Lifting a gentle hand, X softly cupped Arlo’s cheek. This time, when he stared into his eyes, X didn’t see cogs and clockwork, but dreams and a desire for change.
“You want to turn this country on its head, don’t you?”
Arlo’s lips gently curved upward, a sparkle of light returning to his eyes, “How can I allow the SSA to turn one-hundred, if I’m not going to even turn twenty-five?”

X smiled sadly, sorrowful but so immensely proud. “When will you ever rest?”
	“In my grave, Yujin.”

X rushed forward, wrapping his arms around Arlo so tightly that even Time struggled to breathe. Gently, he rested his forehead against Arlo’s own, feeling warm breaths wash over his face. Longing to savor the moment, his eyes drifted shut, drinking in the peace.
Meanwhile, Arlo absorbed the scene with his eyes wide open, busy ingraining every detail of X’s faces into his memory.
“No matter how long I live,” X mused aloud, “I’ll never forget you.”
Arlo huffed, “Be honest, X, you can’t even remember where your car keys are—”
“Let me say something sweet for once!” X protested as he buried his face into Arlo’s chest, red with embarrassment.

Arlo was laughing.
The Epilogue

“Welcome to Channel 9 News! I’m your host, Anila Aiko. Today, the High Congress has passed a new bill called the True Equality Act. It will formally criminalize discrimination on the basis of Spark brightness. Going now to our reporter on the scene: Gale Chapman! How are you, Gale?”
On cue, the camera zoomed in on the man in question, the golden buttons on his navy suit shimmering in the midday light.
“I’m good, Anila!”
“So tell us, what would this landmark bill mean for the country?”

“Well, for starters, it’ll completely overhaul South Korea’s long-standing Spark Classification System instituted by the Spark Separation Act. With this bill in place, citizens can no longer be denied educational or employment opportunities on the grounds of having a dim Spark. Many officials are also optimistic that the homicide rate of lower class citizens, which are currently the highest they’ve ever been, will diminish too as more funding is allocated towards the Bureau of Criminal Investigtation’s Low Class department. On top of that…”
‘No longer will blond boys with ocean eyes feel the need to tear themselves apart for their voice to be heard.’
